title: This breakthrough USB-C cable solves your Mac desktop’s biggest problem
content:
Macworld





USB-C cables have always had a bit of a distance problem. They can carry astonishing amounts of data, drive high-resolution displays, and deliver serious amounts of power—but generally only when the thing at the other end is close by. But imagine the possibilities if the cable was really, really long.
OWC’s new USB4 40Gb/s Active Optical Cables come in 9.8-foot (3 meters) and 16.4-foot (5-meter) lengths, with the latter stretching to about the length as a two-person canoe or an adult saltwater crocodile (pro tip: never mix those two together). What’s remarkable about them is that they can maintain up to 40Gbps of USB4 data throughput over that entire distance. That makes it able to run your Mac’s peripherals much further away then they are now.

				
					

				
			
OWC




How long can a USB-C cable be?
Passive copper cables suffer from signal attenuation and integrity loss over distance. The USB Implementers Forum (USB-IF) has guidelines on USB cable length based on the transfer rate. 5Gbps cables should be at most 6.6 feet (2 meters), while 10Gbps cables can reach up to 3.3 feet (1 meter). This is why the cable you get with your iPhone is 1-meter long,
Though not widely used for data transfer, USB 2.0 cables stretch up to 13.2 feet (4 meters) due to their slow transfer rate of 480Mbps—that’s 83.33 times slower than a 40Gbps connection. If you were transferring a large 50GB file (like a 4K movie), at 40Gbps, the transfer would finish in about 10 seconds. At 480Mbps, the same file would take around 15 minutes to finish.
Passive USB4 and Thunderbolt 3 cables have a maximum length of 3.3 feet (1m), while Thunderbolt 4 maxes out at 6.6 feet (2m). While passive Thunderbolt 5 cables can reach 3 meters, in order to maintain 80Gbps full speed the cable should be maximum 1 meter. Longer setups require active USB4 or Thunderbolt cables that use built-in electronics inside the cable to reach over 2 meters.
The longest 40Gbps cable we’ve seen, from Corning, is actually 82 feet (25 meters), costs over $400, and doesn’t support charging at all. At $130, OWC’s new 16-foot USB4 cables are more reasonably priced and carry up to 240W of power.

				
					

				
			
OWC




How fast is this 16-foot cable?
The physics normally gets in the way. High-speed data doesn’t enjoy travelling long distances through copper. The longer the cable, the harder it becomes to maintain signal integrity at very high frequencies. That’s why passive USB4 and Thunderbolt cables capable of maximum speeds are measured in meters rather than rooms.
OWC’s solution is to replace the traditional copper highway with active multi-mode optical fiber technology. The cable uses light to carry the high-speed data, with active electronics helping maintain the signal over the longer run. It is built for bandwidth intensive applications that require stable, consistent signal transmission and power delivery free from EMI and RFI interference.
The payoff is the impressive bit: 40Gbps over 5 meters.
That’s fast enough for the sorts of things Mac users buy high-speed connectivity for—USB4 and Thunderbolt docking stations, fast RAID storage, PCIe expansion, and high-resolution displays.
Your MacBook doesn’t have to live beside your dock
This is where the cable gets genuinely useful. Want your MacBook on the desk but your noisy external storage tucked away elsewhere? Done. Want the docking station behind the monitor rather than dangling beside the laptop? Easy. Building a cleaner workspace where the computer and peripherals don’t all have to occupy the same few square feet is precisely the point.
You can enhance your cable management by placing AV devices in a rack while keeping your computer at your fingertips, or increase freedom of camera movement by tethering during in-studio shoots. There are even LED indicators at both ends, which indicate that the 16-foot connection is actually working.
The cables support DisplayPort Alt Mode, so they work with compatible USB-C displays as well as Thunderbolt displays. OWC says they’re capable of supporting high-resolution Thunderbolt displays up to 8K, including Apple’s Pro Display XDR and Studio Display.
There is one catch: Fast-charging
Don’t confuse long-distance data performance with far-flung charging. OWC rates its 3-meter cable for up to 240W Power Delivery (easily enough power to fast-charge even the top-end 16-inch MacBook Pro), but the 5-meter version is rated for a reduced 60W. That’s an important distinction for MacBook owners choosing between the two.
60W is close but not quite supported by Apple’s prescribed output for fast-charging. The MacBook Air requires 70W for fast-charging, the 14-inch MacBook Pro demands at least 96W, and the 16-inch Pro won’t charge at its fastest for anything under 140W.
That said, 60W should be plenty to keep even the largest MacBook going as long as it’s not being used to its maximum processing power.

				
					

				
			
OWC




Pricing and availability
You can pre-order the cables at OWC now with the 5-meter cable costing $130 and the 3-meter version costing $99, with general availability scheduled in mid-October.
That’s expensive by average USB-C cable standards—Apple’s 240W USB-C Charge Cable costs $29 but has a maximum bandwidth of just 480Mbps. Thunderbolt costs a bit more, with Apple’s active Thunderbolt 4 Pro Cable (40Gbps) priced at $129 (1.8-meter) and $159 (3 meter).

title: Leaker Jon Prosser Pushes Back as Apple Seeks His YouTube Data
content:
Jon Prosser is arguing that Apple's alleged trade secrets are now public, while the company seeks his YouTube revenue records, channel analytics, and third-party messages to investigate his alleged financial gain from leaks about iOS 26.


In a new joint status report filed yesterday, Apple said it is still waiting for YouTube revenue reports, channel analytics, and third-party communications requested from Prosser more than three months ago. The materials concern his alleged financial gain and how Apple's confidential information was obtained and shared, continuing the discovery dispute detailed in August.

sought to set aside the default against him. He says Apple keeps requesting more documents each time records are produced.

His attorney also argues that Apple's identified trade secrets are now public following the release of ‌iOS 26‌ and macOS 26, and questions whether some were ever secret given earlier third-party disclosures. He says Apple's written descriptions lack corresponding images, making its claims difficult to assess.

Apple disputes that its disclosure is deficient and says it is willing to discuss it with the defendants' lawyers. It also says Prosser's deposition testimony and his Signal exchanges with Michael Ramacciotti suggest the pair coordinated to obtain and disclose confidential information for financial gain, contradicting Ramacciotti's denial of a conspiracy.

Ramacciotti wants to distance his case from Prosser's defense, with his lawyer saying he is "unwilling to be drawn into it." He has asked Judge James Donato for an October conference at which Apple would explain what further evidence it needs, followed by a deadline within 30 days to dismiss its claims against him or commit to trial. He now conditions a second deposition and updated written answers on Apple first providing a roadmap to resolution.

filed the lawsuit in July 2025, alleging that Prosser and Ramacciotti coordinated to access an Apple employee's development iPhone and profit from unreleased software information. Prosser published videos showing recreations of ‌iOS 26‌'s Liquid Glass redesign before Apple's announcement. Apple is seeking damages and an injunction against further disclosure of its trade secrets.

July 2 response to the lawsuit, Prosser admitted participating in a FaceTime call during which Ramacciotti showed him features running on the development device. He denied participating in a coordinated scheme or that the information he viewed constituted trade secrets.

title: Apple’s ‘lighter’ touchscreen MacBook Pro might not be much thinner after all
content:
Macworld





Apple’s imminent MacBook Pro launch offers plenty of reasons to be excited, not least the fact that it’s expected to feature an OLED touchscreen display: the first on an Apple laptop. But one of the other rumored upgrades no longer appears to be on the menu.
Having predicted on multiple occasions that the touchscreen MacBook Pro would be thinner than current models, well-connected leaker Mark Gurman has this week played down that aspect of the redesign. Responding to a tweet on Wednesday night, he expressed doubt about the prospect of it being “significantly thinner” after all.
“Apple is about to redesign [its 16-inch MacBook Pro] in 20 days to be significantly thinner according to Gurman,” the tweet read in part.
“I don’t think it’ll be significantly thinner in the end,” Gurman replied.
This is something of a disappointment, not to mention a change of heart, given statements the leaker made towards the end of last year. In October 2025 he claimed Apple was implementing a thinner and lighter design, having predicted this as long ago as November 2024. Then in November 2025 he yet again said the device would have a “thinner chassis” (subscription required) as well as its OLED display and touch support.
To emphasise the significance of this, Gurman at the time explicitly named the OLED MacBook Pro, along with what turned out to be the MacBook Neo, as Apple products which “mark major shifts.” He contrasted these products with other imminent Mac launches, which he said wouldn’t feature “any major external hardware design changes.”
The good news is that, despite apparently not being noticeably thinner, the device will be noticeably lighter. As recently as this week Gurman said the OLED MacBook Pro would be “significantly lighter” than current models (emphasis his), with a major internal redesign consolidating parts to make it easier to carry. He reiterated that position in the Twitter exchange above, replying at one point with the emphatic, “Lighter!”
The touchscreen MacBook Pro is expected to launch within the next month or so, and could be part of the rumored batch of releases in the last week of October. For all the latest news and rumors, bookmark our regularly updated touchscreen MacBook Pro hub.

title: Best Thunderbolt and USB-C docking stations for your MacBook 2026
content:
Macworld





Plug your MacBook in and out of a multi-port laptop docking station to swiftly add multiple devices and external displays with just one cable connection to your laptop. We tested the top contenders to find the best Thunderbolt and USB-C docks available to owners of the MacBook Air and MacBook Pro. MacBook Neo users can use any of these docks but are limited to a 10Gbps bandwidth and some display limitations.  
Thunderbolt, USB4 or USB-C
The connectors all look the same (technically known as a “Type-C connector”), but there are significant differences, particularly on speed that will determine both data-transfer rate and higher external display refresh rates.
USB-C: 5Gbps or 10Gbps
USB4: 20Gbps or 40Gbps
Thunderbolt 3 and 4: 40Gbps
Thunderbolt 5: 80Gbps / 120Gbps
Our list Which ports does my MacBook have will show you how many USB-C or more likely one of Thunderbolt 3, 4 or 5 that you have.
While a Thunderbolt 4 (TB4) dock will be enough for most casual users, if you can stretch the budget go for a TB5 dock as it will remain current for years, saving you money in the long term, and is backwards compatible with earlier versions and all the way back to USB-C. High-end professionals should always aim for Thunderbolt 5.
The dock needs one (“upstream“) Thunderbolt or USB-C port for connecting to and charging your laptop (although all recent MacBooks can also power via the MagSafe 3 port), and at least another (“downstream“) to attach further devices (hard drives, external display, and others).
The USB-C MacBook Neo has just the one data port, with the other reserved for charging. A dock with Power Delivery will greatly expand the entry-level Mac laptop.
For more detail, read our Thunderbolt 5 vs Thunderbolt 4 vs Thunderbolt 3 vs USB4 explainer.
Add external displays to your MacBook
If you use your laptop as your principal computer, attaching at least one larger display to create a hybrid desktop/laptop setup, with a keyboard and mouse, will boost your productivity. You can turn that 13in MacBook’s cramped screen real-estate into an iconic iMac-sized 27in or even larger screen by adding an extra display—or connect two or even four large monitors to extend your screen across your whole desk. Take a look at our recommended best monitors and displays for Mac and also the best portable monitors for Mac.
You’ll get two or more Extended mode screens (where the screen extends beyond what you can see on the laptop screen) using a Thunderbolt connection (or DisplayPort/HDMI). Natively over mere USB-C, Macs can connect to only one external display in Extended mode, as opposed to Mirrored mode (which replicates exactly what you get on the laptop screen) but DisplayLink is third-party software that allows some docks to extend to up to four screens on even the most basic Mac. DisplayLink-supporting docks are also the only way that non-Pro/Max M1 and M2 MacBooks can connect more than one external display.
More explained: we cover more on Mac docking stations and external displays at the end of this feature below our recommendations.
Do I need a docking station?
With three TB4 or TB5 and an HDMI port, a MacBook with a Max chip could connect to up to four external displays without the need for a dock, although such a power user would likely require extra Thunderbolt and other ports for more devices to make up for using all the laptop ports for multiple monitors. See below our list of recommended docking stations for more detail on the external display options with each recent MacBook.
All docks come with a bunch of USB ports: some old-school USB-A and newer, more capable USB-C. MacBook Pros also have an SD card reader. Although this card reader is rated as UHS-II (312MBps), Apple has pegged it back at 250MBps, so for the fastest speeds (and a microSD slot if you need one), a dock will likely be a better choice for memory-card use if it is rated at UHS-II rather than UHS-I (104MBps).
MacBooks also lack wired Internet access via an Ethernet port, so if you want to escape flaky Wi-Fi, buy a dock with at least Gigabit Ethernet, although you could add a Thunderbolt-to-Ethernet adapter instead if you have a spare TB port. Some later docks include faster 2.5Gb, 5Gb or even 10Gb Ethernet but you’ll need a supporting router or other device to get the benefits, although these faster Ethernet ports are backwards compatible with Gigabit so will future-proof your purchase.
While docking stations are most often attached to MacBooks, they can be useful with a desktop Mac. The Mac mini especially can benefit from the extra ports and built-in SSD slot options. We cover these specifically in our feature on how to upgrade the Mac mini, including reviews of the best hubs and docks that fit the mini. 
Dock or hub?
If you need just a few extra ports, a USB-C hub or Thunderbolt hub might be your best choice—see our roundup of the best USB-C and Thunderbolt hubs for Mac. However, if you require a bunch of fast ports including Gigabit (or faster) Ethernet and multiple video ports plus more powerful charging capability, then look for a full dock that fulfils your needs. We’ve reviewed the best hubs alongside the docks.
USB-C and Thunderbolt speeds

				
					

				
			
Simon Jary / Foundry




• USB and Thunderbolt speeds explained
USB PD: Power Delivery for your laptop
Most docks can charge the connected MacBook, so look for the right Power Delivery (PD) rating that suits your laptop. You can’t over-power a MacBook so the simplest advice is to aim as high as you can. 70W will be more than enough to fast-charge a MacBook Air but go for 85W or more (PD 3.0) for a MacBook Pro, and 140W (PD 3.1) for the top-end 16-inch Pro.
We’ve got more detailed advice on recommended MacBook charging speeds below our list of docks.
Best docks for Mac 2026
Here we list the Thunderbolt and USB-C docks that we have reviewed and tested. Read the descriptions for details on all the features and functions offered by each docking station.
We start with the latest Thunderbolt 5 docks as they offer the most but docks with TB4 might well be all you need and often (not always) come in cheaper. The benefit of buying a Thunderbolt 5 dock now—even if your Mac doesn’t have it—is that it’s backwards compatible and future proofs you for your next Mac purchase.
You can save money by choosing a Thunderbolt 4 or even USB-C docking station, the best of which are also reviewed in this chart.

If you desire the ultimate in MacBook docking stations, the CalDigit TS5 Plus has just about everything you need—indeed probably more than you need. Alongside super-fast Thunderbolt 5 you get an incredible number of top-end ports including 10Gb Ethernet and an incredible 330W power supply. Somehow CalDigit has included an incredible clearly labelled 20 ports into the compact dock—all of which can be used simultaneously—including ten 10Gbps USB ports (five USB-C and five USB-A), the fastest Ethernet available, top-rated card readers and audio ports front and back. There are three 80Gbps Thunderbolt 5 ports: one upstream to connect to your computer and two downstream for speedy data-transfer devices.
CalDigit has sacrificed a possible third downstream TB5 port for a dedicated DisplayPort in the knowledge that most dock users run at least one external display and so the extra TB5 port would be used for a monitor connection anyway. The TS5 Plus is the first dock with dual 10Gbps USB controllers, one controller for the front ports and one for the ports at the back of the dock for increased USB bandwidth. Each of the USB ports offers 7.5W of power except the front-facing 36W USB-C port. The two downstream Thunderbolt 5 ports also offer 36W. While the CalDigit TS5 Plus has just about everything you need, the iVanky FusionDock Ultra probably does have everything and a whole bunch more. This dock is for high-end Mac professionals who need maximum connectivity, especially those running multiple high-resolution displays, fast storage and 10Gb networking all at once.
The advantage this dock has over other Thunderbolt 5 docks is its dual Thunderbolt 5 chips, making it effectively two docks in one case. Using two upstream Thunderbolt connections also provides significantly more bandwidth, avoiding the bottlenecks that often occur with single-port docks. The downside is that you must use two of your Mac’s Thunderbolt ports to use the FusionDock Ultra. If only one cable is connected, some ports on the dock will not function.
The Ultra can natively deliver up to four external displays—a feat that usually takes a docking station that requires third-party DisplayLink compression software to be installed on the Mac. Not including the backwards-compatible Thunderbolt ports, the FusionDock Ultra carries a mind-boggling 12 plainer USB ports: all at 10Gbps.

The only thing that lets this dock down is its weak 149W power supply. The Staechi and Plugable rivals both have 180W power supplies.

A KVM docking station enables you to instantly share a single set of peripherals—the KVM stands for Keyboard, Video (monitors) and Mouse—between two computers. While most docks allow you to connect different computers, a KVM dock makes it easier with a special “Switch”—a button that you push to instantly take control from the other computer. The KVM Switch virtually disconnects the first computer and connects the second without you having to unplug any cables.
The iDock M10 from AV Access is a Mac-dedicated KVM dock that you can connect to a MacBook and a desktop computer, including a Windows PC. It comes with a KVM Wired Remote Controller, which is the button you press to toggle between computers. The dock features 15 ports but four of them are used as upstream connections to the two computers. 
Setup requires two MacBook Thunderbolt ports and dedicated connections to both computers. Major limitations include weak device charging, limited port flexibility, no support for two laptops,

Who should buy the iDock M10?
This dock is not aimed at most Mac users, but if you have a shared setup of one MacBook and one desktop Windows PC or a desktop Mac (mini or Studio), the KVM functionality of the iDock M10 comes into its own when those two computers are sharing the same dual displays and input devices at different times.

							
		
Which ports are on each MacBook?
Of Apple’s recent laptop ranges, the M1/M2/M3 MacBook Air and 14-inch M3 MacBook Pro feature two ports that Apple specified as “Thunderbolt / USB 4” ports, while more recent the 13in and 15in M4/M5 MacBook Air models feature two Thunderbolt 4 ports. The 14in and 16in M1/M2/M3 Pro, plain M4/M5 MacBook Pro, and M1/M2/M3 Max MacBook Pro models come with three Thunderbolt 4 (TB4) ports. Ignore Apple’s dual designation of non-4 Thunderbolt and USB4—it just means that the ports don’t certify as pure Thunderbolt 4, and that shouldn’t worry most users except for the number of external displays each supports.
Apple’s latest M4/M5 Pro and M4/M5 Max MacBook Pro models feature three of the latest Thunderbolt 5 ports, which are backwards compatible with TB4, TB3 and USB-C. They promise 80Gbps data transfer and 120Gbps video rates. Until the technology finds its way into more devices and the Thunderbolt 5 dock market matures, you are still going to do very well with a 40Gbps Thunderbolt 4 dock, but Thunderbolt 5 docks are fast becoming the norm for new releases.
Thunderbolt 5 frees the latest top-end M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBooks from the two-display limitation forced on them by the macOS’s lack of MST (Multi Stream Transport) support. The M5 Pro now supports up to three external displays over a single Thunderbolt connection and the M5 Max up to four. To reach four external displays most docks reviewed here would need to daisy-chain the fourth display off one of the others.
The entry-level MacBook Neo utilizes lower-spec USB-C rather than Thunderbolt, with 10Gbps rather than Thunderbolt’s 40Gbps or 80Gbps. A USB-C dock is therefore all you should need but it will work with Thunderbolt, which is backwards compatible, but limited to the Neo’s 10Gbps bandwidth.

				
					

				
			The latest MacBook Pro models boast three Thunderbolt 5 ports.
Apple

How many external displays can each MacBook support without a dock?

M4: Supports up to two external displays over a single Thunderbolt port, one with up to 6K resolution at 60Hz and one at 5K/60Hz.
M5: Supports up to two external displays over a single Thunderbolt port, one with up to 6K resolution at 60Hz and one at 6K/60Hz.
M1/M2/M3/M4 Pro: Up to two external displays with up to 6K resolution at 60Hz over Thunderbolt, or one external display with up to 6K resolution at 60Hz over Thunderbolt and one external display with up to 4K resolution at 144Hz over HDMI. Or one external display supported at 8K resolution at 60Hz or one external display at 4K resolution at 240Hz over HDMI.
M1/M2/M3/M4 Max: Up to four external displays: Up to three external displays with 6K resolution at 60Hz over Thunderbolt and one external display with up to 4K resolution at 144Hz over HDMI. Up to three external displays: Up to two external displays with 6K resolution at 60Hz over Thunderbolt and one external display with up to 8K resolution at 60Hz or one external display with 4K resolution at 240Hz over HDMI.
M5 Pro: Supports up to three external displays over a single Thunderbolt port. Up to three displays up to a native resolution of 6K (6144 x 3456) at 60Hz or 4K (3840 x 2160) at 144Hz over Thunderbolt or HDMI. Or one external display supported at 8K (7680 x 4320) at 60Hz, 5K (5120 x 2880) at 120Hz, or 4K (3840 x 2160) at 240Hz, plus a second display up to a native resolution of 5K (5120 x 2880) at 120Hz or 4K (3840 x 2160) at 200Hz over Thunderbolt or HDMI.

Mac docking stations and external displays

				
					

				
			
Baseus




While Apple’s MacBooks featuring the company’s own M-series Silicon chips are super speedy compared to the models sporting Intel processors, models with plain (non-Pro or -Max) M1 and M2 chips come with an incredible limitation: they don’t support more than one external display in Extended Mode even via their Thunderbolt ports. Plain M3 MacBooks can support two displays but only with their lids closed. The MacBook Neo uses a different A18 Pro chip and has the same single-monitor limitation as the plain M1 and M2.
This limitation means that when using any docking station, M1/M2 and Neo MacBook users cannot extend their desktop over two or more displays, and will be limited to either dual Mirrored displays or one external display—although adding third-party DisplayLink or InstantView software to the Mac and connecting to a dedicated USB-C dock will allow you to add more than one external monitor to an M1, M2 or M3 MacBook. Follow that link for our roundup of the best USB-C DisplayLink docks, and we’ve included our favorite in our roundup above.
In the example above, standard M1/M2/Neo Macs would require DisplayLink to achieve Extended Mode 2. M1/M2/M3/M4 Pro/Max and standard M3/M4/M5 onwards can natively work in that mode without DisplayLink but would require it for three or more extended screens. M5 Pro supports three screens, and M5 Max supports four, without requiring DisplayLink.
Above, we’ve listed the native external display options for each MacBook. Thunderbolt 5 docks should support up to four 6K displays if you own an M5 Max-chip MacBook Pro.
While some docking stations promise support for 8K displays, Macs are limited to 6K support via the dock. Macs with an M2/M3/M4 Pro or Max chip can support an 8K display at 60Hz but only when it is connected via the Mac’s own HDMI port and not any port on the dock.
Dock, hub or dongle: Whole lotta ports
You need one (“upstream“) Thunderbolt or USB-C port for connecting to and charging your laptop (although the 14/16in MacBooks can also power via the MagSafe port), and likely at least another (“downstream“) to attach further devices (hard drives, external display, and others).
There are many inexpensive USB-C dongles/hubs that let you add more devices to a MacBook (see our roundup of the best USB-C adapters for Macs) or a Thunderbolt hub offering a few extra ports might be all your need, but for maximum flexibility check out a docking station that takes care of all your extra port requirements, and allows you to simply attach it to your laptop with just one cable when you get to the office or come home.
Docks aren’t just for MacBooks. Mac mini (2018 and later) and iMac (2017 and later) owners may also consider expanding their ports with a Thunderbolt docking station.
The inclusion of an SD or microSD card reader isn’t just for camera buffs. It’s a convenient and affordable way to add storage to your laptop setup. We found a 512GB Samsung Evo microSD card on Amazon for around $100 in the US and under £100 in the UK. That’s a very cheap way of adding half a terabyte of portable storage. For more details read up on our best microSD cards.
Some of the docks reviewed above include an integrated SSD enclosure that lets you add up to 8TB of fast storage to your connected MacBook.
Charging the laptop
While the MacBook Neo can get by on 20W Power Delivery (PD), the M1/M2/M3/M4/M5 MacBook Air requires a PD charger with at least 30W power, but you can fast-charge an M2 and later Air with a charger rated at over 70W. You’ll need 67W for the 13-inch MacBook Pro and 70W for the 14-inch MBP (with 8-, 10-, 11-or 12-core CPU), 96W for 14-inch MBP (with 12- or 14-core CPU), and 96W (preferably 140W) for the 16-inch MBP. The older 15in MacBook Pro requires a 87W PD charger.
If you own a larger MacBook Pro, buy a dock with a PD (Power Delivery) potential of at least 85W if you can. USB PD 3.0 maxes at 100W, while USB PD 3.1 can support up to 240W of power. The 16-inch MacBook Pro requires 140W to fast-charge, so owners of that laptop should look for a PD 3.1 charger.
If you just need a spare charger, we’ve tested the best MacBook chargers for you.
Other dock options
Here we concentrate on Thunderbolt docks, but also include cheaper USB-C docks—which Thunderbolt MacBooks can use, but at the cost of reduced bandwidth and display limitations. We’ve also included our favorite Thunderbolt hubs for smaller and cheaper alternatives. For more non-Thunderbolt USB-C-only docks check out Tech Advisor’s roundup of the best USB-C docking stations for laptops. Tech Advisor also reviews all the available Thunderbolt 4 docks.
Now think about a stand to go alongside the dock
These MacBook docking stations look and work great with a laptop stand, and we’ve also tested some MacBook-friendly stands that lack all the extra ports but keep your MacBook/Air/Pro upright and out of the way: further saving valuable desk space, reducing clutter, keeping your laptop cool, and saving it from spills.

title: Surface Laptop Ultra is Microsoft’s best effort to catch up to Apple
content:
Macworld





On Wednesday, Microsoft introduced the Surface Laptop Ultra, the first laptop to ship with Nvidia’s new RTX Spark processor (there will be offerings from other companies like HP and Lenovo, too). At a glance, it seems pretty clear that they’re gunning for Apple. 
Up to 20 ARM-based CPU cores and a big fat Nvidia Blackwell GPU with up to 6,144 cores (Nvidia and Apple count GPU cores very differently). A big bright HDR display, from 24GB to 128GB of RAM, and SSDs from 512GB to 2TB… this is Microsoft’s version of a MacBook Pro, all right. Even the price is somewhere in line with a 16-inch M5 Pro MacBook Pro: it starts at $2,599, but that’s for a version of the chip with fewer cores and will a 512GB SSD, half what you get in the base model of the 16-inch MacBook Pro.
These systems are being pitched at developers working with local AI models, some of which take tens of gigabytes of memory. During Microsoft’s presentation, models as big as 60GB were touted, and the 128GB unified memory maximum was hyped as a key benefit. That sounds very much like Apple’s MacBook Pro pitch these days.
Specs between the two systems are very hard to compare, as neither company really lists comparable features or performance figures. But let’s take the full-size RTX Spark laptop and stack it up next to the 16-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Max:


M5 Max MacBook ProRTX Spark Surface Ultra

Price as configured$6,999$5,899
CPU cores18 cores (6 super, 12 performance)20 cores (10 performance, 10 efficiency)
GPU cores40 cores6,144 cores
RAM128 GB (614 GB/sec)128 GB (300 GB/sec)
SSD2 TB1 TB

 



You currently can’t get more than a 1TB SSD in the Surface Ultra if you choose the full-size processor with all the CPU and GPU cores. And you can’t get less than a 2TB drive from Apple in the 16-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Max with all its cores. But in other configurations, Microsoft charges $400 more for the 2TB SSD.
The chip specs are equally hard to compare, because the cores are different, and performance claims don’t use the same figures. But we can get some idea of relative CPU performance by looking at the benchmarks of the DGX Spark, which is a Linux-based desktop system that uses a version of the chip with identical specs as the RTX spark. The RTX Spark is basically the DGX Spark made for Windows 11 ARM laptops. 
There’s a reason why Microsoft compared it to the M5 Pro. Apple’s M5 Max CPU absolutely crushes the DGX Spark CPU in Geekbench. Nvidia’s chip gets a single-core score of ~2,600 and multi-core score of ~23,700. Apple lands at ~3,700 single-core and ~35,600 multi-core. Yeah, 40-50 percent faster. I don’t think Apple has anything to worry about.
The GPU is where it gets more interesting. Both Apple and Nvidia have GPUs that are optimized for doing AI work, but they don’t list comparable specs. Nvidia claims 1 petaflop of FP4 performance, but you won’t find maximum performance specs using that format for Apple’s chip. 

				
					

				
			Nvidia unveiled the RTX Spark at Computex in May, and the first laptops are just about to hit the market.
Adam Patrick Murray / Foundry




Nvidia claims about 100 teraflops of FP16 performance for the DGX Spark, so the RTX Spark should be similar. That figure for the M5 Max is about 70 teraflops. But Nvidia’s architecture is well-optimized for small, compact, quantized models using small data formats, and should handily beat Apple with those.
On the other hand, Apple’s M5 Max has more than twice the memory bandwidth. Depending on the model or data it accesses, memory bandwidth can quickly become the bottleneck. So for certain AI tasks, the M5 Max’s 614 GB/sec is going to give it a big advantage.
The Surface Ultra runs Windows 11 for ARM, which requires ARM-optimized applications to run at peak performance, and provides a sort of translation layer (called Prism) to run non-native apps. Right now, the vast majority of Windows apps are made for x86 processors and don’t have native ARM versions. That’s not really an issue for Apple, which is all but done with its ARM-based Apple Silicon transition. Nearly all Mac apps run natively on M-series processors, and Rosetta 2 is really only necessary for old software.
There are, of course, a lot of other considerations here. Microsoft’s laptop has a touchscreen, while the MacBook Pro does not (not yet, at least). Ports, battery life, charging speed, speakers and microphones, keyboard and trackpad quality, webcam quality… a laptop is so much more than its processor.
Apple has a big head start on AI software, too. Agentic AI research and deployment has been all over the Mac, since Apple has offered consumer-grade hardware with lots of unified, high-bandwidth memory for years. Researchers and businesses have been buying up Mac minis and Mac Studios with high memory pools as fast as they can to run big models locally. There’s a reason all the consumer “agent” AI apps, from Meta’s Muse or Claude Desktop start off on the Mac and come to Windows later. 

				
					

				
			
The Surface Ultra laptop has a nice processor and design, but it remains to be seen how it stacks up to the MacBook’s battery and build quality. 

Mark Hachman / Foundry




Microsoft even just announced a new Windows framework for the local inferencing of AI models called “Windows ML” that supports models from PyTorch, TensorFlow/Keras, TFLite, scikit-learn, and others. That sounds exactly like the current function of the CoreML framework that Apple first introduced way back in 2017.
Ultimately, Apple doesn’t need to worry about the Surface Ultra or other RTX Spark laptops just yet. Those computers are all very expensive, and there’s no affordable option with the same architecture. Apple has Mac laptops from $1,299 that all use the same major processor architecture, operating system, APIs, and so on. At the end of the day, people buy Windows laptops (ARM-based or not) because they want to run Windows, and the buy Macs because they want to run macOS. 
But RTX Spark laptops like the Surface Ultra do show that Apple was on the right track the whole time: A single energy-efficient processor with a lot of ARM cores, a powerful GPU, and a big pool of unified memory? That sounds exactly like what Apple has been delivering to customers for years.

Apple’s HomePod lineup could be about to undergo its biggest expansion since the original HomePod launched. Apple is reportedly preparing a new HomePod mini and smart home display for October 13, with another full-size HomePod expected further down the line, as it builds a new generation of home products around Siri AI.
For much of 2025 and 2026, Apple’s revamped Siri was the thing holding those products back. That’s no longer the case: Siri AI has now arrived with Apple’s OS 27 updates, removing one of the biggest obstacles to launching the new hardware. The HomePod mini 2 appears to be particularly close, with Apple code discovered in September 2026 revealing images of the unreleased speaker and its five colors, while Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported in July that a new HomePod mini, Apple TV and smart home display are among Apple’s upcoming home products.
The naming is less straightforward. “HomePad,” “Smart Home Hub,” “Personal Hub” and “HomePod Touch” are all placeholder names being used for different rumored products or concepts, rather than confirmed Apple names. In this article, we’re using “HomePad,” “Smart Home Hub” and “Personal Hub” for the standalone smart display reportedly being developed for smart-home controls, Siri AI and video calls, while “HomePod Touch” refers specifically to reports about a HomePod-style speaker with an integrated touchscreen.
There may ultimately be some overlap between these products, and some of the rumored concepts could be combined, renamed or never released at all. Below, we separate what is currently known about each device and when it is likely to arrive.




						

							




What are the new HomePod products?
Apple is reportedly developing several new HomePod and smart-home products. The names below aren’t official Apple names; where necessary, we’re using placeholder names to distinguish between the different rumored devices.


Placeholder nameWhat is it When 

HomePod mini 2New HomePod mini with the same basic design, new colors, faster processor and Siri AI support.October 13, 2026 (rumored)
HomePad/Smart Home Hub6-inch smart display with Siri AI, Home controls, apps and camera; tabletop and wall-mounted versions expected.October 13, 2026 (rumored)
HomePod 3Next-generation full-size HomePod with faster hardware and Siri AI supportIn development, but reportedly not imminent
HomePod TouchHomePod with a built-in 6-inch touchscreen.Uncertain; no firm launch window
Robotic home screen Display mounted on a robotic arm 2027 or beyond
Security cameraApple-designed home security cameraTiming uncertain
LG smart-home accessoriesReported Apple/LG collaboration on a doorbell, lock, thermostat and security camerasOctober 13 announcement rumored; availability potentially months later

 






Why have Apple’s new Home products taken so long?
Apple’s next generation of smart-home products appears to have been delayed largely because of Siri. The company was developing a much more capable version of Siri for Apple Intelligence, while the processors inside the current HomePod mini and second-generation HomePod weren’t designed to run Apple’s latest AI features.
That created a problem for new HomePod hardware. Apple was reportedly preparing products such as a new HomePod mini and smart home display around the capabilities of the redesigned assistant, but Siri’s delayed development meant the hardware couldn’t launch as originally expected.
That situation has now changed. Siri AI arrived with Apple’s OS 27 updates in September 2026, removing one of the main dependencies that had been holding back Apple’s smart-home plans. Recent reports suggest the HomePod mini 2 and Apple’s smart home display are among the products closest to release.
The full-size HomePod appears to be on a different timetable, however. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported in September that Apple is testing a new full-size HomePod with Siri AI support, but said it “doesn’t appear to be imminent.” That means we no longer expect the HomePod 3 to necessarily arrive alongside the HomePod mini 2.


						

							







HomePod mini 2 rumors
We’ll start off with the rumors about the HomePod mini 2. The HomePod mini is Apple’s smaller, more affordable smart speaker. The new model is expected to offer a new selection of colors, a major processor upgrade and improved connectivity.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




When is the HomePod mini 2 expected to launch?
October 13, 2026 rumored; unconfirmed
Apple introduced the original HomePod mini in November 2020, so it is now nearly six years old and overdue for an update.
Rumours of a successor have circulated for more than a year. In January 2025, reports suggested a launch toward the end of 2025, and Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman subsequently said that new HomePod mini and Apple TV models were expected in fall 2025. Those products never materialised.
Attention then shifted to spring 2026, with reports suggesting Apple’s new smart home devices would launch alongside its redesigned Siri. However, that timetable also slipped as Apple continued work on its AI-powered assistant.
If those plans remain on schedule, the HomePod mini 2 is expected to launch alongside Apple’s broader refresh of its smart home lineup this fall, with most reports pointing to October.
What changes are coming to the HomePod mini 2?
Black, blue, green, pink, and white color finishes.
The current HomePod mini is available in Midnight, White, Blue, Yellow and Orange. In September, MacRumors spotted Apple code that revealed five colors for the new model: black, blue, green, pink, and white.
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported in September 2025, that Apple has tested additional colors for the next-generation model, including red, but it appears that red didn’t make the final cut. 
Otherwise, the HomePod mini 2 is expected to retain the same compact, spherical design as the current model, with no major external changes rumored. Instead, Apple is reportedly focusing on upgraded internal hardware, including an S9 or newer chip capable of supporting Apple’s latest Siri AI features.
Other changes coming to HomePod mini 2
Beyond the color changes revealed in Apple code, the main expected hardware upgrade is a newer processor capable of supporting Siri AI. Reports also point to newer Apple networking and Ultra Wideband hardware, along with possible audio improvements.
Siri AI support: A newer processor should allow the HomePod mini 2 to support Apple’s latest Siri AI features, something the current S5-based model wasn’t designed for.
Improved connectivity: Reports have pointed to Apple’s newer in-house networking hardware, Wi-Fi 6E and an upgraded Ultra Wideband chip.
Audio improvements: Apple is expected to upgrade the speaker’s audio hardware and processing.
Other internal upgrades: Further hardware refinements are possible.


						

							


HomePad/Smart Home Hub rumors
Possible launch: October 13, 2026, according to Bloomberg
Strategy: A new smart-home display category for Apple
HomePad release date 
Apple’s first smart home display could launch on October 13, 2026. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports that Apple plans to introduce its new smart-home products on that date, with the long-rumored home hub expected to be the centerpiece of the launch. 
There are signs that Apple could make an announcement even earlier. Confidential retail-display boxes have arrived in Apple Stores, reportedly marked for opening on October 8. This suggests that a product launch is imminent, although it is unclear what the materials relate to. The iPhone Duo goes on sale October 23, so October 8 would appear too early to be connected to that.
Apple has not confirmed the date, and Gurman’s report does not say whether the products will be unveiled at an event or announced through Apple’s website. 
The product had originally been expected earlier in 2026, but its launch was repeatedly pushed back while Apple completed the Siri AI technology that arrived with its September OS 27 updates. Gurman previously reported that the hardware had been ready for some time, with Siri the main reason for the delay.
Apple’s own software has also provided evidence that the product is approaching launch. References discovered in macOS identify J490/HomeAccessory17,1 and J491/HomeAccessory17,2, which are believed to correspond to the tabletop and wall-mounted versions of Apple’s smart home hub.
Earlier reports had only narrowed the launch window to 2026, while a March post from leaker Kosutami hinted at a fall release. Those reports have now been superseded by Gurman’s more specific October 13 timeframe.
What is the HomePad?
The HomePad – also referred to as Apple’s Smart Home Hub or home display – is expected to be a compact 6-inch smart display designed to act as a central interface for the home. It would combine Siri AI, smart-home controls, FaceTime, media playback and Apple services in a device intended to remain plugged in on a countertop, desk, bedside table or wall.
The latest reports suggest that it will be considerably smaller than many earlier concept images implied. A six-inch square display would measure only about 4.25 inches across each side, making it much more of a close-up personal device than an iPad-sized family display. It is likely to be more “desk scale” than “room scale.” 
Apple’s new Siri AI is expected to be central to the HomePad experience. Its delayed development appears to have been one of the main reasons the hardware did not launch earlier.

				
					

				
			
Foundry / ChatGPT




HomePad design, features and specs
Reported features include:
6-inch display: The latest Bloomberg report points to a six-inch display with rounded corners, making the device considerably smaller than many earlier renders suggested.
iMac G4-style tabletop design: The standard model is reportedly mounted above a circular metal speaker base on a polished metal arm, with a design said to be reminiscent of the classic iMac G4. 
Colors: Leaker itspdfu has suggested Rose Pink, Silver, Space Gray and Starlight based on Photo Face setup assets.
Tilting display: The screen is reportedly designed to tilt forward and backward manually.
Wall-mounted version: A second model is reportedly designed to mount on a wall, with a thin square base containing the speakers and microphones.
No battery: The device is expected to remain plugged in, reportedly using USB-C for power.
Siri AI: Apple’s new Siri technology is expected to be central to the device.
Smart-home controls: It should act as a central interface for Home accessories.
FaceTime and communication: A front-facing camera is expected to support FaceTime calls.
User recognition: The device is reportedly designed to recognize household members by face and voice, then display that person’s own calendar, reminders, notes and other information.
Visitor mode: Reports suggest it will be able to hide personal information when guests are using the device.
iPhone authentication: A nearby iPhone may be used for stronger authentication when required.
Other software clues and reports suggest the device could also offer:
Apple apps and services: Reports specifically mention Calendar, Messages, Photos, FaceTime, Notes, Reminders, Music, Podcasts and smart-home controls.
Entertainment: The device is also expected to function as an entertainment hub for streaming music and video, as well as making FaceTime calls via a built-in camera.
New home-focused software: The device is reportedly running a new interface combining elements of Apple Watch, Apple TV and iPhone/iPad software, including widgets, clock faces and photo displays rather than simply running iPadOS. 
No App Store expected at launch: Current reports do not mention an App Store, suggesting the HomePad may initially operate more like a dedicated smart-home appliance than a general-purpose iPad.
Other clues about HomePad software:
Kitchen integration: A new “CookingKit” framework and expanded food sections in Apple News indicate that kitchen assistance, such as searching for recipes by ingredient, could be a primary selling point.
Advanced home control: Code found in the iOS 26 Home app describes an “Adaptive Temperature” feature, which could allow the HomePad to offer more granular control over smart thermostats, including energy-saving optimizations based on local electricity rates.


						

							


HomePod 3 rumors
The larger HomePod is more expensive than the HomePod mini, delivering richer, louder audio with deeper bass and spatial audio. The next generation is expected to get a processor upgrade, improved connectivity and better sound.

				
					

				
			
Michael Brown/Foundry




When is the HomePod 3 expected to launch?
Release date: Unknown; not expected imminently
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported in September 2026 that Apple was testing a new full-size HomePod with Siri AI support, but that the release did not appear to be imminent.
What changes are coming to the HomePod 3?
Unlike the HomePod mini 2, there are relatively few leaks about hardware upgrades coming to the full-size HomePod. However, it’s expected to receive the same core internal upgrades needed to support Apple’s AI ambitions.
Expected improvements include: 
More powerful chip: The current HomePod uses the S7 chip from the Apple Watch Series 7. A next-generation model is expected to adopt a significantly faster Apple silicon chip, potentially the S9 or newer, to support Apple Intelligence features.
Siri AI support: The upgraded hardware should allow the HomePod to run Apple’s new Siri AI features that aren’t supported by the current S7-based model.
Improved Connectivity: Rumours point to Apple’s in-house networking chip, together with Wi-Fi 6E and an upgraded Ultra Wideband chip for improved performance and smart home integration.
Audio Enhancements: Apple is also expected to refine the speaker system with upgraded drivers and audio processing.
In September, a post by itspdfu, who has a history of posting leaks online, said that audioOS27, the operating system for HomePod devices, supports Siri AI. The same source claimed that a future HomePod could also include new animations for its top display.
Beyond these internal upgrades, some reports suggest Apple is experimenting with a HomePod featuring a built-in display. That device is expected to be a separate product rather than a standard HomePod 3, and we cover those rumours in the next section.


						

							


HomePod with touchscreen (HomePod Touch) rumors
Apple has been rumored to be working on a HomePod with a screen for years, although exactly what form that product will take remains unclear. Older reports have described a HomePod-style speaker with an integrated touchscreen, sometimes referred to unofficially as a “HomePod Touch.”
There is considerable uncertainty here because some older reports about a “HomePod with a display” may describe the same product that more recent reports characterize as Apple’s HomePad or smart home hub. We are treating the HomePod Touch separately here only where reports specifically describe a HomePod-style speaker with an integrated screen.

				
					

				
			
Foundry and Apple




When could the touchscreen HomePod launch?
Possible launch: Unknown
Apple has been working on redesigning the HomePod to include a display for some time. Back in March 2023, analyst Ming-Chi Kuo claimed Apple would “unveil a redesigned HomePod featuring a 7-inch panel.” Kuo initially expected this product to arrive in the first half of 2024, but that timeline slipped. In December 2024, he reported further delays had pushed the launch to after WWDC 2025, citing software development challenges. Then, in March 2025, Kuo suggested the device had been delayed again, due to Apple Intelligence setbacks.
Those predictions have all passed without a product appearing. Siri AI has since arrived, but there is currently no firm report giving this touchscreen HomePod a new launch date. It is therefore possible that earlier reports referred to a product that has evolved, been delayed further, or overlaps with Apple’s separately reported HomePad project.

				
					

				
			
HomePod with display incoming?

Foundry




What could the touchscreen HomePod be like?
Display size: 6 and 7-inch touchscreens.
Software: Custom touchscreen operating system running apps like Weather, Calendar, Photos, HomeKit as well as Apple Music
One of the biggest limitations of today’s HomePod is that almost every interaction relies on Siri. A built-in display would provide a more direct way to control music, manage smart home devices and access information, putting Apple’s device in direct competition with the Amazon Echo Show and Google Nest Hub.
According to current rumours, Apple’s display-equipped HomePod will feature a 6-7-inch touchscreen and run a touch-optimised version of homeOS, allowing it to function as both a smart speaker and a smart home hub. Unlike existing HomePods, it is expected to use a far more powerful A-series chip – possibly an A18 or similar – to support Apple’s redesigned AI-powered Siri and the more demanding graphical interface.
Rumoured features:
Large touchscreen: A 6-7-inch display for controlling smart home devices, viewing photos, checking the weather, following recipes and interacting with apps.
Powerful Apple silicon: An A-series chip is expected to replace the S-series processor used in current HomePods, providing the performance needed for Apple Intelligence and the touchscreen interface.
Smart-home controls: A touchscreen HomePod would logically offer easier access to Home controls, although reports about apps and a dedicated smart-home interface may refer instead to Apple’s separate HomePad project
Improved connectivity: Apple’s in-house networking chip, Wi-Fi 6E and an upgraded Ultra Wideband chip are all rumoured.
FaceTime camera: Reports suggest Apple may include a built-in camera for FaceTime and other video-based features. These could instead relate to Apple’s separate HomePad project.
Possible modular design: Some less-established reports have suggested that a display could dock with a speaker base. This has not been corroborated by the more recent reports describing Apple’s HomePad.
If accurate, this would represent Apple’s biggest expansion of the HomePod lineup since its debut, transforming it from a voice-first speaker into a full smart home controller.

				
					

				
			Amazon Echo Show beside the HomePod mini, 
Ben Patterson/Foundry



							


Apple robotic home display rumors
Possible launch: 2027 or later
Strategy: A premium smart-home device with a movable display
Apple is also developing a much more ambitious smart-home device that shouldn’t be confused with the HomePad expected first (see above).
As far back as April 2021, Mark Gurman described a high-end device combining a HomePod speaker, a touchscreen, and a camera mounted on a robotic arm that could follow the user around the room during video calls. Gurman has made various references to this over the years.
The device, previously identified as J595, is reportedly an iPad-like display attached to a motorized robotic arm. The arm would allow the screen to move and reposition itself, potentially following a person around the room during FaceTime calls or turning toward whoever is speaking.
Bloomberg has described it as a higher-end smart-home command center that could combine videoconferencing, home controls and security functions. Unlike the stationary HomePad, this appears to be a significantly more complex—and probably more expensive—product. Earlier reports have suggested a price that could reach around $1,000.
The robotic display is also believed to be further away than the HomePad. Previous reports placed it in late 2026 or 2027 at the earliest, and Apple’s more recent software leaks have focused on the J490 and J491 stationary home hubs rather than J595.
What could the robotic display do?
Reported capabilities include:
A large display mounted on a motorized arm.
Automatically turning toward the person using it.
FaceTime and other video calling.
Siri AI and smart-home controls.
Cameras and gesture recognition
Reports suggest cameras could support FaceTime, security monitoring and potentially recognition of users or gestures. Apple has also previously filed patents describing HomePod-related gesture controls, although patents do not necessarily indicate features destined for a shipping product.


						

							


Associated LG accessories 
There is a rumor that LG accessories could accompany Apple’s smart-home launch
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports that Apple is working with LG on a doorbell, smart lock, thermostat and security cameras. These accessories could be announced on October 13, but reportedly would not reach customers for several more months.
The products are expected to carry LG branding, with LG handling manufacturing and support. They are separate from the Apple-branded accessories also rumored to be in development. A separate leak from itspdfu points to an LG temperature and humidity sensor. 


						

							


What chips will power the new HomePods?
The biggest limitation of today’s HomePods isn’t their speakers – it’s their processors. The HomePod mini still uses the Apple Watch S5 chip introduced in 2019, while the second-generation HomePod runs on the newer, but still relatively modest, S7 chip from the Apple Watch Series 7.
Those chips are powerful enough for music playback, Home controls and existing Siri functions, but they were not designed to run the new Siri AI capabilities introduced with Apple’s OS 27 generation.
That hardware gap helps explain why Apple is expected to introduce new HomePod hardware rather than bringing the full Siri AI experience to the existing models.
HomePod mini 2 & HomePod 3
Gurman has said the main hardware change he has specifically reported for the new HomePods is a faster chip, although he has not identified which processor Apple will use.
HomePod with a screen
The display-equipped HomePod is expected to require substantially more processing power than Apple’s existing smart speakers. Because it will reportedly run a touch-based operating system alongside Apple Intelligence, most analysts expect it to use an A-series processor, with an A17 Pro or A18 among the leading predictions. Apple has not confirmed the chip, and these reports remain speculative.
Whatever processors Apple ultimately chooses, the goal appears to be the same across the entire HomePod range: replacing ageing Apple Watch chips with modern Apple silicon capable of delivering the full Apple Intelligence experience.


						

							


New HomePod Prices
The prices for the HomePods increased in June 2026:
HomePod: $349/£349 (was $299/£299)
HomePod mini: $129/£129 (was $99/£99)
Apple raised HomePod prices in June 2026, so we wouldn’t expect the new models to return automatically to the previous $99/$299 price points.
However, a HomePod with a built-in screen could command a higher price. It may launch as a separate product altogether, potentially starting around $399/£399, or higher, depending on features.


						

							


Buying advice: Should you wait or buy a HomePod now? 
Wait if: You are considering a HomePod mini. A replacement now appears close, with reports pointing to fall 2026 and Apple code already revealing the unreleased model.
Buy now if: You need a HomePod immediately and find a worthwhile discount. The current HomePod and HomePod mini still work well as speakers and smart-home hubs, but their older processors mean they aren’t designed for Apple’s newer Siri AI capabilities.
If you want a screen: Wait. Apple’s first dedicated home display appears much closer than the more speculative touchscreen HomePod.


						

							


What is on Apple’s Smart Home Roadmap
October 2026: The HomePod mini 2 is expected, with October currently the leading possibility.
October 2026: Apple’s HomePad/smart home display could also launch, although its timing is less certain.
Beyond 2026: A new full-size HomePod is being tested, but Bloomberg reports that it does not appear imminent.
2027 or later: Apple’s more ambitious robotic home display could follow.
Timing unknown: Apple is also reportedly developing home-security camera hardware.

title: Apple Watch Series 12 & Ultra 4: Everything you need to know about the 2026 Apple Watches
content:
Macworld





In September 2026 Apple unveiled the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4, with both models focusing much more heavily on health monitoring, Apple Intelligence and battery efficiency than on physical redesigns. Series 12 remains Apple’s mainstream premium smartwatch, while Ultra 4 continues as the larger, tougher model aimed at endurance sports, outdoor activities and diving. Both Apple Watches went on sale on September 18.
The biggest upgrade shared by both watches is Apple’s all-new Health Sensing System, which combines redesigned optical and electrical heart sensors with larger, more power-efficient green LEDs. Apple says it provides the most accurate heart-rate sensing of any wearable it tested. Background heart-rate readings are now taken every five seconds, while HRV can be measured as often as every five minutes – 60 times and 24 times more frequently respectively than on Series 11.
That additional data powers another major addition: Readiness, which gives users a 0–10 score based on recent activity, sleep, vitals and recovery data, and updates during the day. Both watches also use Apple’s new S11 chip, which enables Siri AI and a collection of Audio Intelligence features including Sound Recognition, faster Shazam, Live Rewind and Siri Recap. Live Rewind and Siri Recap are not available yet. Apple says both will arrive as beta features later in 2026, initially in English.
The most dramatic hardware improvement is reserved for the Ultra 4: Apple has increased its normal-use battery-life rating from 42 hours to 50 hours, Low Power Mode from 72 to 84 hours, and introduced workout modes capable of tracking for up to 45 hours. Series 12 remains rated at 24 hours, although our testing found inconsistent battery life and charging performance, while the aluminium Series 12 gains tougher Ceramic Shield 2 and Apple has brought back a premium ceramic Apple Watch for the first time in years.
The five biggest Apple Watch upgrades for 2026
New Health Sensing System with substantially more frequent heart-rate and HRV monitoring.
Readiness score for daily recovery and training guidance. 
S11 chip, Siri AI and Audio Intelligence, including Siri Recap and Live Rewind, which are both coming in a later software update.
Much longer Ultra 4 battery life, rising from 42 to 50 hours, with up to 45 hours of extended workout tracking.
New materials and durability, including Ceramic Shield 2 on aluminium Series 12 and the return of ceramic Series 12 models.
The rumours were broadly right that this wouldn’t be a major redesign, and also correctly predicted the emphasis on health, Siri AI and ceramic materials. However, rumours of Touch ID have not materialised, there is still no blood-glucose sensor, and the Series 12 hasn’t gained longer quoted battery life despite speculation about a larger battery. Starting prices are unchanged, although the 46mm Series 12 costs more.

				
					

				
			
Your watch knows how you are feeling. Do you? 

Apple




Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4: Top 10 features


FeatureApple Watch Series 12Apple Watch Ultra 4

Health Sensing SystemNew optical/electrical sensorsSame new system
Background heart rateEvery 5 secondsEvery 5 seconds
HRVAs often as every 5 minutesAs often as every 5 minutes
Readiness scoreYesYes, with training data
ProcessorS11S11
Siri AIYesYes
Audio IntelligenceSupported; Live Rewind and Siri Recap await an English-language beta later in 2026Supported; Live Rewind and Siri Recap await an English-language beta later in 2026
Display42mm/46mm, up to 2,000 nits49mm, up to 3,000 nits
BatteryUp to 24 hours; 38 hours Low PowerUp to 50 hours; 84 hours Low Power
SatelliteNo direct satellite communicationsEmergency SOS and Find My via satellite

 






Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 release date and availability
Apple announced the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 on September 9, 2026. Both models went on sale on September 18 and are available from Apple, authorized retailers and participating carriers.
watchOS 27 was released on September 14 for compatible existing Apple Watches.
Both watches are available now, including in the U.S., U.K., Australia, Canada and more than 50 other countries and regions.
You can buy them directly from Apple through Apple.com, the Apple Store app and Apple retail stores. They are also available through Apple-authorised retailers and, in the case of cellular models, participating mobile networks.
$349.99 at  Amazon										 | 
																$399 at  Walmart						
					
$774 at  Amazon										 | 
																$774 at  Walmart										 | 
																$799 at  Best Buy US						
					
Buy Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 at Apple U.S. 
Buy Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 at Apple U.K. 


							


Apple Watch Series 12 design

				
					

				
			
The Apple Watch Series 12 in bronze.

David Price / Foundry




The Series 12 does not represent a major external redesign, as the pre-launch rumours suggested. It retains Apple’s familiar rounded-square design and comes in 42mm and 46mm sizes.
Interestingly, the aluminium and titanium cases are fractionally wider than Series 11. The 46mm model measures 46 x 40 x 9.7mm, compared with 46 x 39 x 9.7mm for Series 11. The 42mm version measures 42 x 37 x 9.7mm, compared with 42 x 36 x 9.7mm previously. The screen resolutions remain 416×496 pixels and 374×446 pixels respectively.
Apple continues to offer aluminium and titanium models, but ceramic has returned as a premium case option. Ceramic models are fractionally larger and thicker, measuring 43mm or 47mm tall and 9.85mm thick.
The finishes are:
Aluminium: Dark Bronze, Light Gold, Black and Space Grey
Titanium: Radiant Gold and Natural
Ceramic: Pearl White and Night Blue
The ceramic options confirm one of the more interesting pre-launch rumours, although Apple opted for Night Blue rather than the dark grey that had also been indicated.
The Series 12 display remains a wide-angle LTPO3 Always-On Retina OLED with up to 2,000 nits brightness. Aluminium models now use Ceramic Shield 2, which Apple says is 60 percent tougher than the Ion-X glass used on Series 11. Titanium and ceramic versions use sapphire crystal.


						

							


Apple Watch Ultra 4 design

				
					

				
			
The rugged Apple Watch Ultra 4.

Apple




The Ultra 4 changes even less externally. It remains a 49mm Grade 5 titanium watch, measuring exactly 49 x 44 x 12mm, with the same 422×514-pixel display and 1,245 sq mm display area as Ultra 3.
It comes in the familiar Natural Titanium and Black Titanium finishes and retains its flat sapphire crystal display, raised protective case edges, prominent Digital Crown and orange-accented Action button.
The Ultra 4 is slightly heavier, however: 63.0g in Natural and 63.1g in Black, compared with 61.6g and 61.8g respectively for Ultra 3.
The display remains a wide-angle LTPO3 Always-On Retina display capable of 3,000 nits, so there is no headline screen-brightness upgrade.
Apple hasn’t introduced the rumoured Touch ID fingerprint sensor on the 2026 Apple Watch models. 


						

							


What about the buttons and controls?

				
					

				
			
The side button.

Apple




The physical control layout is essentially unchanged.
Series 12 has:
Digital Crown with haptic feedback
Side button
Strap-release buttons
Ultra 4 adds the familiar:
Customisable Action button
Larger protected Digital Crown
Side button
The Action button can start workouts, mark segments, move to the next interval, activate the torch and perform other user-selected actions.
There is, however, a new single-tap finger-and-thumb gesture in addition to Double Tap and Wrist Flick, providing another way to interact without touching the display.


						

							


Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 processor: What processor do they use?
Both watches use Apple’s new S11 chip, replacing the S10 used by Series 11 and Ultra 3.
Apple’s specifications list:
64-bit dual-core processor
4-core Neural Engine
64GB storage
Secure hardware for Audio Intelligence processing
The S10 also had a 64-bit dual-core CPU, four-core Neural Engine and 64GB of storage, so the headline specifications alone don’t reveal how much faster S11 actually is. Apple calls it its “most powerful wearable chip”, but notably hasn’t provided a percentage CPU or GPU performance improvement over S10, and its technical specifications don’t list a separate GPU core count.
That means the more important S11 improvements appear to be what the chip enables rather than raw benchmark performance.
It works with the new Health Sensing System, supports Siri AI and powers the new Audio Intelligence functionality. Apple has also emphasised efficiency, particularly in relation to higher-frequency sensor readings and Ultra 4’s improved battery life.
The new Audio Intelligence system includes a Secure Exclave, a hardware-isolated area of the S11 that processes audio separately and deletes raw audio immediately after processing.


						

							


2026 Apple Watch connectivity

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




Connectivity changes are modest. Cellular Series 12 and Ultra 4 models support 5G RedCap and LTE, as did their predecessors, with no newly branded Apple-designed modem.
Both watches also support Wi-Fi 4 (802.11n) on 2.4GHz and 5GHz, Bluetooth 5.3, and Apple’s second-generation Ultra Wideband chip. Wi-Fi 4 may sound dated, but Apple Watch relies mainly on Bluetooth and has relatively low data requirements.
Satellite connectivity
Satellite communications remain a major distinction between the Series and Ultra families.
Apple Watch Series 12 doesn’t have built-in satellite connectivity.
Ultra 4 does, supporting Emergency SOS via satellite and Find My location sharing via satellite when cellular and Wi-Fi aren’t available.
This is broadly what had been expected before launch: satellite remains primarily an Ultra feature rather than migrating to the regular Series watch.


						

							


2026 Apple Watch battery and charging: What’s new?

				
					

				
			
Charging the Apple Watch. 

Apple




Apple Watch Series 12
Apple rates Series 12 for:
Up to 24 hours normal use
Up to 38 hours in Low Power Mode
Up to 10 hours of outdoor workout tracking
Those first two figures are unchanged from Series 11, so despite rumours that Apple was working on a larger battery, there is no increase in Apple’s quoted everyday battery life.
Apple claims improved endurance from a short charge.
Apple quotes the following charging figures for Series 12:
80 percent in around 30 minutes
Up to 12 hours of use from a 15-minute charge
Up to 10 hours of sleep tracking from five minutes of charging
Apple also rated Series 11 for an 80 percent charge in around 30 minutes, and up to eight hours of normal use from a 15-minute charge.
In our Apple Watch Series 12 review, we recorded 51 and 40 hours of battery life across two runs – an average of 45.5 hours, compared with 47.5 hours for Series 11. Charging also varied: our watch reached 58% and 72% after 30 minutes in separate tests, falling short of Apple’s claimed 80%. These results show that the Series 12 can comfortably exceed Apple’s 24-hour rating, but they don’t demonstrate a consistent improvement over Series 11. Actual battery life depends on usage.
Apple Watch Ultra 4
Battery life is one of Ultra 4’s biggest upgrades.
Apple rates it for:
50 hours normal use, up from 42 hours
84 hours Low Power Mode, up from 72 hours
18 hours standard outdoor workout tracking
25 hours Extended Workout
45 hours Max Extended Workout
Apple says the Extended Workout figure represents a 25 percent increase over the previous generation.
Apple says Ultra 4 can reach 80 percent in around 45 minutes, but 15 minutes of charging now provides up to 18 hours of use, versus 12 hours on Ultra 3.
Apple also credits more efficient workout algorithms with helping deliver the longer endurance.
Apple Watch charging
Both models use Apple’s magnetic fast-charging system with the Apple Watch Magnetic Fast Charger to USB-C Cable.
There is no conventional wired charging port on either watch and no change to the basic magnetic charging system this year.


						

							




Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 price
Apple has kept its entry prices unchanged in both the U.S. and U.K. – contrary to pre-event speculation that the Series 12 could increase in price.


Model2026 pricePrevious generation

Series 12 – U.S.42mm $399 / 46mm $449Series 11: 42mm $399 / 46mm $429
Series 12 – U.K.42mm £369 / 46mm £419Series 11: 42mm £369 / 46mm £399
Ultra 4 – U.S.From $799Ultra 3: $799
Ultra 4 – U.K.From £749Ultra 3: £749

 



Series 12 pricing varies considerably depending on case material. Aluminium is the entry-level option, while titanium costs more and the newly revived ceramic models occupy the premium end of the range.
Starting prices are unchanged, but the larger Series 12 costs more. The 46mm aluminum model starts at $449/£419 with GPS or $549/£519 with cellular—an increase of $20/£20 over the equivalent Series 11 models.
Should you buy Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4?

				
					

				
			
Apple




Apple Watch Series 12 is the best choice for most people. It offers essentially all of Apple’s important new features – including the new Health Sensing System, Readiness, frequent HRV measurements, Siri AI and Audio Intelligence – in a considerably smaller and cheaper watch. (Live Rewind and Siri Recap are not available yet.)
However, our Series 12 review found inconsistent battery life and charging, along with occasional sluggishness. These observations may not reflect an established problem affecting every watch, but they temper our recommendation, particularly for owners of recent models considering an upgrade.
The strongest reason to choose Ultra 4 is battery life. IIts increase in Apple’s rated battery life from 42 to 50 hours makes it much more practical for people who regularly spend more than a day away from a charger, while the new 25- and 45-hour extended workout modes make it substantially more appealing to runners, hikers, cyclists and endurance athletes.
Ultra 4 is also the better choice for outdoor adventurers because of its brighter 3,000-nit display, dual-frequency GPS, rugged titanium construction, Action button, 100m water resistance, recreational diving support and satellite communications. Series 12 is the better everyday watch: lighter, less bulky, available in two sizes and substantially cheaper.

title: New iPad Mini Rumored to Have 60Hz OLED Display Ahead of Launch
content:
Ahead of the expected imminent launch of the new iPad mini 8, word out of Asia suggests that the device will feature a 60Hz OLED display rather than a ProMotion 120Hz display.


The information comes courtesy of a hit-and-miss tipster running the account "yeux1122" on the Korean Naver blog. "There have been mentions of 120Hz in some overseas reports, but the domestic production quantity has already been confirmed to be LTPS at 60Hz," the tipster wrote. "That's it."

claimed they had been told by a source in Apple's supply chain that the unreleased iPad mini is equipped with a low-temperature polycrystalline silicon (LTPS) backplane hybrid OLED panel clocked at 60Hz.

Apple's ‌iPad Pro‌ models feature two-stack low-temperature polycrystalline oxide (LTPO) OLED panels‌, which makes the display capable of dynamically adjusting its refresh rate between 10Hz and 120Hz (aka ProMotion). In contrast, LTPS OLED panels are usually paired with fixed refresh rates – such as 60Hz, 90Hz, or 120Hz – and are typically dimmer than LTPO panels.

If the leak is true, it's likely to disappoint iPad mini fans. Previous reports have not been clear on whether the iPad mini 8 will feature a higher refresh rate than the 60Hz LCD display used in the existing iPad mini 7. Given that the base iPhone 17 uses a 120Hz ProMotion panel, some would have believed it was reasonable to expect the same on the first OLED iPad mini. That said, the iPhone 17e goes to show that Apple is still in the 60Hz OLED business, so it might not consider the iPad mini to be a big enough market to justify the more advanced panel technology.

title: Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 Score 4/10 for Repairability
content:
Repair site iFixit this week continued taking apart the latest Apple devices, this time tearing down the Apple Watch Series 12 and the Apple Watch Ultra 4.



The ‌Apple Watch Ultra 4‌ has no repairability changes. There are copious amounts of glue between the casing and the display for waterproofing, and getting to the battery has to be done through the screen. It's easy to slice through the display cable when attempting to pry the device open.

The Apple Watch Series 12 is also difficult to get into, but it has a pull tab for the adhesive holding the battery in place, which iFixit says is a "modest" repairability improvement. The Series 12 also drops the ZIF connector that made repairs more difficult, which makes for a simpler process. There is no way to access the battery without removing the display, and no way to swap the display without removing the battery.

The ‌Apple Watch Ultra 4‌ has a 2.444Wh battery, up from 2.313Wh in the Apple Watch Ultra 3. The 46mm Series 12 has a 1.461Wh battery, up from 1.403Wh for the Series 11.

With the pull tab and the improved cable layout, iFixit gave the Apple Watch Series 12 a repairability score of 4 out of 10, an improvement over the last base model iFixit scored. The Ultra 4 also earned a 4 out of 10, which is the same score iFixit has given to all prior Apple Watch Ultra models.

The site points to Google as proof that a wearable can be repairable. Google's Pixel Watch 5 earned a repairability score of 9 out of 10. The Pixel Watch 5's display and battery can be accessed by removing a few screws and a gasket, with no adhesive to deal with.

iFixit claims Apple is "out of compliance" with the Right to Repair laws in Washington, Oregon, California, Nevada, Colorado, Minnesota, Texas, New York, Maryland, and Connecticut because it does not sell Apple Watch repair parts or service tools, nor does it offer repair manuals.

title: Apple Watch Series 12, Ultra 4 Owners Report Skin Irritation
content:
Some Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 owners have experienced unexpected skin irritation with the new models, according to reports on the MacRumors forums and Reddit.


Affected users complain of a burning sensation and redness under the sensor area. The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 measure heart rate every five seconds, and some people have wondered if that's the cause of the skin irritation.

Along with more frequent heart rate readings, the Series 12 and Ultra 4 have a larger ECG electrode surface, photodiodes in a ring-shaped arrangement, and larger green LEDs. It is unknown if any of these design changes are a problem, but wrist irritation from the Apple Watch is a complaint that dates back to the original model.

Apple says reactions can be caused by wearing a band too tight or too loose, or by irritants like soap and sweat under the watch. Some Apple Watch models contain nickel, but it is a low amount below EU limits, and Apple says it's unlikely to be a problem. The Apple Watch case and certain Apple Watch bands have trace amounts of acrylates and methacrylates from adhesives, but Apple says it designs the watch and bands to keep those components away from skin.

Apple recommends making sure a band fits well and keeping the Apple Watch, bands, and skin clean and dry. Apple adds that cleaning may be required after workouts or exposure to liquids like sweat, soap, sunscreen, and lotion.
